title: C3808 — Seat climate inline connector guide
introduction:
A climate-controlled seat has more electrical conversation going on than its cozy reputation suggests. This inline connector reference includes heater, temperature-sensor, blower-control, fan and network labels. I use the Function column to separate those jobs before following a circuit identifier; a heater connection and a temperature-sensing connection answer different questions.

Choose the gender and harness heading first. In that section, find a cavity label in the drawing and read across the corresponding table row. Circuit Number identifies the circuit, Color records its wire-color code, Function describes the connection’s role, and Terminal Part Number identifies the listed terminal. Keep heater and fan polarity symbols attached to their original functions.

The male drawing has its lower-numbered group on the left, while the female drawing reverses those groups. Gray-filled positions correspond to blank circuit and function entries in their tables. Housing projections provide visual landmarks, without labeled release or locking functions. Several corresponding male and female rows name different functions; those differences remain unresolved, so the tables cannot yet be treated as a verified continuous circuit map.

This reference teaches identification, with access, disconnection, probing and repair left to the applicable service procedure. The physical viewing side, Gauge convention and meanings of Size and Used codes are unspecified. Preserve the printed entries without converting them into wire-selection advice, test limits or fault conclusions.

edits.why: I pair the harness identity with this drawing before locating a cavity. The separated corner positions and numbered columns are useful landmarks within the illustration; the drawing does not identify the physical side from which to view a connector.

The function descriptions distinguish heater polarity, cushion-temperature sensing, switch and indicator connections, blower-speed control, fan polarity and network communication. Keeping those roles separate prevents a shared housing from being mistaken for a shared electrical purpose.

The numbered groups occupy the opposite sides from those in the male illustration. I read this face’s own labels rather than transferring left-and-right positions. Its larger side projection is an outline feature whose operating function is unspecified.

Read the female table independently, retaining its heater, cushion and back temperature, blower-control, network and fan descriptions. Some functions differ from the male listings at corresponding positions; neither table supplies the qualifier needed to reconcile them.

Keep each kit’s service part, engineering shell, material, gauge and cavity fields together as a separate catalog entry. The two entries for the male shell have different kit and service-part numbers; sharing a shell number does not establish interchangeability or select a repair kit. These listings do not provide installation instructions.

The Product Id is a separate regional catalog listing. The table does not associate it with a particular kit row above or supply installation instructions; do not infer either association from its placement.

originalAuthorHold: Corresponding face assignments conflict at cavity 5: male CHS14 is passenger indicator high, while female VHS35 is driver back temperature sensing; at cavity 6: male CHS29 is the front-driver seat-heater switch, while female RHS15 is driver back-temperature sensor circuitry; and at cavity 10: male CHS09 is passenger indicator low, while female VHS16 is driver back-blower speed control. No supplied applicability qualifier resolves these differences.

editorialRevision.scope: Complete independent active-agent review of all 72 primary units, four complete pages/two figures and six edits. Original first CLI author covered 60 units/four headings. Complete draft adds pigtail and European catalog headings, all table rows and raw text coverage. Original partial author retained separately; physical seat-control assignments and gauge conventions remain unresolved for bounded source reading only.
